abstract.chunk: Contents lists available at Science Direct journal homepage: /locate/oceaneng A novel context-aware deep learning framework for ship radiated noise recognition Di Zeng a,b, Yuning Li c, Xianli Pan c,∗, Shefeng Yan a,b a Institute of Acoustics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, 100190, China b University of Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, 100049, China c Capital Normal University, Beijing, 100048, China a r t i c l e i n f o Keywords: Ship radiated noise classiﬁcation Context-Aware learning Deep learning a b s t r a c t Existing methods for Ship Radiated Noise (SRN) classiﬁcation primarily focus on feature extraction and model design based solely on acoustic data, which limits further performance improvements. To overcome this limitation, we propose CA-SRNNet, a context-aware deep learning framework that integrates both temporal and semantic information to enhance SRN classiﬁcation. Speciﬁcally, a time-aware varying-coeﬃcient regression module is introduced to dynamically incorporate temporal context, allowing the model to adapt feature representations over time. Additionally, ship category labels are leveraged to guide representation learning via a semantic-aware contrastive loss. We employ Bayes error bound analysis to demonstrate the framework’s superior feature extraction capability and use SHAP to quantify the contribution of the temporal module.

introduction.chunk: Accurately classifying Ship Radiated Noise (SRN) holds signiﬁcant importance in national defense and economic security Wang et al. The complexity of this task arises from pervasive environmental noise and substantial intraclass variability among similar types of vessels Xie et al. Developing advanced and eﬀective classiﬁcation algorithms remains a crucial and challenging area of research. Numerous methods have been developed to address the challenges of classifying SRN. Traditional machine learning techniques, such as Support Vector Machines (SVM), Random Forests (RF), and K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) Bansal et al. (2022), have been widely used due to their eﬀectiveness in leveraging handcrafted features Liu et al. However, these approaches are generally more suited for small-scale datasets with limited feature diversity, as they rely heavily on manual feature extraction Lin et al. (2023), Mumuni and Mumuni (2024). In contrast, deep learning models have gained prominence by automatically learning hierarchical feature representations and capturing complex nonlinear patterns in large-scale SRN data. Beneﬁting from advances in hardware acceleration and optimized training frameworks, deep learning models have become increasingly feasible and widely adopted in SRN classiﬁcation, demonstrating superior performance over traditional methods Shiri et al. The design of these two modules is guided by the characteristics of the dataset used in our experiments.1 However, the framework is highly ﬂexible and generalizable.2 1 We conduct our experiments on two public SRN benchmarks, Deep Ship and Ships Ear, both of which provide ship-radiated noise recordings together with metadata such as timestamps and ship category labels. These contextual attributes provide a natural basis for incorporating temporal and semantic information into the learning framework. 2 The contextual inputs used in CA-SRNNet are modular and data-dependent. Although this study focuses on the recording time and ship category, the frame Moreover, CA-SRNNet supports interchangeable backbone architectures, allowing it to be tailored to a wide range of model capacities and deployment requirements. This modularity enables CA-SRNNet to serve as a uniﬁed and extensible solution for diverse SRN classiﬁcation tasks. We proceed to describe the two modules in detail and discuss how their combined design improves SRN classiﬁcation. Temporal feature encoding and integration In real-world underwater acoustic measurements, time-related metadata (e.g., year, month, day, hour, minute, second, or coarse seasonal tags) is almost always available. From an underwater acoustics perspective, such temporal variables are not merely bookkeeping information: diurnal and seasonal cycles modulate water temperature, stratiﬁcation, and surface mixing, thereby aﬀecting sound-speed proﬁles, multipath structure, and the ambient noise ﬁeld; in parallel, shipping, ﬁshing, and tourism activities follow time-dependent schedules that change the prior occurrence of diﬀerent vessel classes. In other words, timestamps provide a cheap but informative proxy for a mixture of environmental and anthropogenic factors.

We adopt a stratiﬁed 5-fold cross-validation protocol on the Deep Ship dataset to ensure balanced and fair evaluation. Within each class, recordings are sorted by duration and distributed across folds in a round-robin manner. To prevent data leakage, all clips originating from the same recording are assigned to a single fold.3 For the Ships Ear dataset, where the number of recordings is relatively small, we construct a single recording-level train-test split following the same nonleakage principle. The resulting per-class distributions for Deep Ship and Ships Ear are summarized in Table 2 and Table 3, respectively. To improve statistical reliability, each experiment is repeated ten times with diﬀerent random seeds. Evaluation is performed on the test set of each fold, and ﬁnal results are reported as the average classiﬁcation accuracy across all folds and repetitions. All experiments are conducted on a server with an Intel Xeon Gold 6330 CPU and an NVIDIA RTX 3090 GPU (24 GB VRAM). 3 Some existing studies randomly split short-time clips derived from the same audio ﬁle into the training, validation, and test sets, which often leads to overly optimistic test accuracies exceeding 95 %. We apply BN-BER to assess the theoretical error rates of features extracted by CA-SRNNet and three representative baselines: Res Net-18, CFTANet, and RCMo E-balance. 4 shows the BER estimates across varying values of the truncation threshold parameter 𝜏 (from 1 to 9), which controls the proportion of samples treated as reliable during noise estimation. Following the guidance in Chen et al. (2023), we perform a full sweep over 𝜏 due to its notable inﬂuence on the ﬁnal estimate. Across all conﬁgurations, the CA-SRNNet-enhanced variants consistently achieve lower BER values than their unmodiﬁed counterparts, especially at higher 𝜏 levels where the estimation stabilizes. This indicates that the features learned with contextual integration exhibit stronger class separability and reduced intrinsic uncertainty. In summary, our theoretical analysis using BER provides evidence that the proposed context-aware modules not only improve empirical classiﬁcation accuracy, but also enhance the quality of learned representations in a principled manner. This conﬁrms the dual beneﬁt of our framework: empirical eﬀectiveness and theoretical soundness. Interpretability analysis To shed light on how CA-SRNNet exploits contextual information and class semantics, we perform two complementary interpretability studies: SHAP-based temporal feature attribution and semantic-acoustic alignment analysis based on BERT embeddings and learned acoustic representations.

Although CA-SRNNet is designed as a generic context-aware framework that can, in principle, accommodate any encodable metadata, it still requires that the types and coverage of contextual variables be comparable between training and deployment. In its current form, the model does not directly transfer to a new scene with diﬀerent sensor types, regions, or ship classes without adaptation, as illustrated by the need to retrain on the Ships Ear dataset. The practical advantage of the proposed architecture lies in its modular design: context always enters through learnable embeddings and lightweight conditioning modules that are decoupled from the acoustic backbone. When new operational conditions or 347 (2026) 123891 12 D. Zeng et al. ship categories are introduced, one can incorporate new context codes and update primarily the context-related parameters (or a small set of adapter layers), while keeping most backbone weights ﬁxed. In this way, online adaptation or cross-domain transfer can be implemented via targeted ﬁne-tuning of the context branch, rather than full retraining of the entire network. Environmental factors and current limitations. From a physical standpoint, the temporal context used in CA-SRNNet is closely related to underlying environmental and anthropogenic factors: changes in season, time of day, and human activity patterns all inﬂuence sound-speed structure, ambient noise, and thus the received SRN. In a ﬁxed coastal region, calendar time is typically associated with diﬀerent water-temperature and salinity regimes, which in turn shape the sound-speed proﬁle and the way ship noise propagates and attenuates; at the same time, time of day and season correlate with sea state and traﬃc intensity, and therefore with background noise level and scattering conditions.

methodology.chunk: methods for Ship Radiated Noise (SRN) classiﬁcation primarily focus on feature extraction and model design based solely on acoustic data, which limits further performance improvements. To overcome this limitation, we propose CA-SRNNet, a context-aware deep learning framework that integrates both temporal and semantic information to enhance SRN classiﬁcation. Speciﬁcally, a time-aware varying-coeﬃcient regression module is introduced to dynamically incorporate temporal context, allowing the model to adapt feature representations over time. Additionally, ship category labels are leveraged to guide representation learning via a semantic-aware contrastive loss. We employ Bayes error bound analysis to demonstrate the framework’s superior feature extraction capability and use SHAP to quantify the contribution of the temporal module.

results.chunk: experiments across multiple backbone networks consistently show improved classiﬁcation performance, conﬁrming the eﬀectiveness and generalizability of the proposed approach.

conclusion.chunk: We propose CA-SRNNet, a context-aware deep learning framework for SRN classiﬁcation, which integrates temporal and semantic information through two key modules: Temporal Feature Encoding and Semantic-Guided Contrastive Learning. These components are jointly optimized with the backbone network in an end-to-end manner, allowing contextual signals to inform both feature extraction and ﬁnal decision-making. Extensive experiments across multiple time-frequency representations and backbone architectures demonstrate consistent and signiﬁcant improvements in classiﬁcation performance. Furthermore, Bayes error rate estimation and SHAP-based interpretability analysis provide theoretical and diagnostic evidence supporting the effectiveness of our context-aware design. The results conﬁrm that CA-SRNNet not only enhances classiﬁcation accuracy, but also facilitates the learning of more structured and predictable feature spaces.
